title: High-Status Leaders Who Do What They Ask of Others
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Jim Fish, CEO of the largest waste management company in the United States, rides along with trash crews and attends 1 a.m. safety briefings about 20 times per year. The principle illustrated by Fish's actions is clear: the greater the status difference between leader and team, the more powerful the message when leaders willingly do what they ask of others. Through direct engagement with drivers and frontline workers, Fish discovered a critical safety problem affecting the entire organization: when English-only managers had safety talks translated into Spanish for Spanish-speaking workers, crucial nuance was lost in translation. By deliberately hiring and promoting bilingual managers, he transformed the company's safety record. The broader lesson is that high-status leaders build credibility and gain critical insights not through delegation and distance, but through humble, deliberate participation in the work they oversee.
points: The greater the status gap between leader and team, the more impactful it becomes when leaders do what they ask of others
Direct engagement with frontline workers reveals insights and problems that corporate headquarters might never understand otherwise
Leaders who demonstrate willingness to perform everyday tasks gain extraordinary credibility and trust throughout their organization
Fish's personal listening to workers uncovered a fundamental and organization-wide language barrier affecting safety outcomes
Visible, occasional participation in actual work transforms how leaders are perceived, listened to, and followed across the organization
quotes: Fish knows something about leadership that is worth remembering. The more status a leader holds, the more important it is for them to demonstrate their willingness to do what they ask of others.
People respond differently to leaders who go out of their way to do the everyday tasks they ask of others.
Fish's credibility throughout the organization is off the charts because he demonstrated genuine willingness to participate.
Trust is the outcome for high-status leaders who do what they ask of others.
He learns this insight by showing up and talking openly with team members who trusted him.” Archived from Admired Leadership Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
